title: Can you generate AI images on an iPhone with no internet?
body:
Yes — with one condition that nobody mentions up front: the model has to get onto your phone first, and it is large. After that, everything happens on the device and the internet is genuinely irrelevant.

What "on-device" actually means

Most AI image apps are a text box wired to somebody else's computer. You type, your words travel to a server, a graphics card there draws the picture, and it travels back. That is why they meter you — every image costs them real money — and why they stop working on a plane.

An on-device generator puts the model itself on your phone and runs it on Apple's Neural Engine, the chip built for this work. Nothing is sent anywhere. The picture is drawn a few inches from your hand.

The trade you are actually making

You are trading storage and setup time for having no limits and no server.

  • A one-time download of roughly 3 GB. That is the model. It happens once, over Wi-Fi, and never again.
  • A first-launch wait of about two minutes. iOS compiles the model for the Neural Engine the first time. It is unavoidable — Apple provides no way to skip or pre-warm it — and it happens once per install.
  • A modern device. This is the real gate, and it has its own guide.

What you get back: no credit counter, no queue, no account, and it works in a basement, on a flight, or anywhere with no signal at all.

How to check whether it is genuinely offline

Do not take anyone's word for it, including ours. Install the app, let it finish its download, then turn on airplane mode and generate something. If a picture appears, the claim is true. If you get an error, the app was a client for a server the whole time.

What on-device generation is not good at

Being honest about this is more useful than another list of benefits. A phone-sized model is roughly a generation behind what a desktop graphics card runs. It follows long, complicated prompts less precisely, and it will not render text inside an image reliably. If you need a specific paragraph rendered inside a poster, cloud tools are still better at that.

What it is good at is everything else — and doing it without asking permission, without a subscription, and without stopping at image three.

title: Will your iPhone or iPad run an on-device image generator?
body:
The honest answer is memory, not age. A recent budget phone can fail where an older expensive one succeeds, because what matters is how much RAM the device has — and Apple does not print that number anywhere a normal person will find it.

The number that decides it

An SDXL-class image model needs around 6 GB of memory to load and run. Below that, the model cannot be compiled for the Neural Engine at all. It does not run slowly — it does not run.

Standard model 6 GB an iPhone 14 or later, an iPhone 12 Pro or 13 Pro, or an iPad with an M-series chip Higher-detail 12 GB an iPhone or iPad with at least 12 GB of memory

The pattern to notice: Pro models carry more memory than the standard model of the same year. An iPhone 12 Pro works where an iPhone 12 does not.

Why there are two tiers

Drawing at a higher resolution costs memory roughly in proportion to the number of pixels. A model that draws at 1024 across needs meaningfully more headroom than one drawing at 768 — enough that a device clearing the first bar can still fail the second. That is not a marketing tier; it is arithmetic.

Storage, which people forget

Budget around 3 GB per model, plus room for what iOS keeps after compiling it for the Neural Engine. If your phone is permanently at 2 GB free, this category is not for you yet, whatever chip you have.

What a well-built app should do about it

It should check before it downloads anything, and say which devices work in plain words rather than showing you a technical error after a 3 GB download. If an app lets you download three gigabytes and only then fails, that is a bug and worth a refund request.

If your device does not qualify

Cloud generators run on anything, because the work happens elsewhere. You give up the offline part and accept credits or a subscription. That is a real trade, not a consolation — for an older phone it is the only option that works.

title: How to upscale a photo to 4K on your iPhone
body:
Enlarging a photo and upscaling a photo are different operations, and the difference is why one looks soft and the other does not.

Resizing versus upscaling

When you resize an image, the software spreads the pixels it already has over a larger area and guesses the gaps by averaging neighbours. Nothing is added. A blurry photo becomes a larger blurry photo.

An upscaling model has been trained on millions of pairs of small and large versions of the same picture. It has learned what fabric weave, hair, brickwork and foliage look like close up, so it reconstructs plausible detail rather than averaging. That is why the result looks sharp rather than smooth.

What this can and cannot do

It is very good at texture: skin, fur, fabric, stone, leaves. It is good at edges that were soft because the image was small rather than because the shot was out of focus.

It cannot recover information that was never captured. A photo taken out of focus stays out of focus — sharper, but still wrong. A face too small to be more than a few pixels will not become a recognisable person; the model will invent a plausible one. And upscaling a heavily compressed image will faithfully sharpen the compression artefacts along with everything else.

Doing it on the phone, offline

Upscaling runs comfortably on modern Apple hardware, and unlike generation it does not need a huge model — the one we use is about 33 MB and ships inside the app, so it works from the moment you install and never touches the network.

Practically: pick the picture, choose how much larger you want it, and let it run. Output is capped at 4096 pixels on the longest side, which is more than enough for a large print or a desktop wallpaper. On an M-series iPad, a full 4096-pixel result takes roughly ten to twelve seconds.

Why size is a choice, not a maximum

Bigger is not always better. If you want a cleaner version of a picture at the size it already is, ask for 1× — you get the detail reconstruction without the file becoming enormous. Doubling is usually the sweet spot for something you will look at on a screen. Reach for the maximum when you are printing.

Adjusting afterwards

A sharper picture often wants small corrections — a little more warmth, the shadows lifted, the highlights pulled back. Doing that after upscaling rather than before means the adjustments apply to the detail that was reconstructed, not to the softer original.

title: How to write better prompts for AI image generation
body:
Most prompting advice tells you to add more words. That advice is wrong, and understanding why will fix more of your images than any list of magic phrases.

There is a hard limit, and you will hit it sooner than you think

The model stops reading at about 60 words. Everything after that is thrown away — not treated as less important, thrown away. If your carefully considered lighting note sits at the end of a long prompt, the model never saw it at all.

The exact figure is 77 of what the model calls tokens, which are roughly words but not exactly: common words cost one each, unusual ones cost two or three. So "a red fox at night" is five, while a long compound word might be four on its own. Sixty words is the number to keep in your head.

This produces a failure that feels like the model ignoring you, when really you were cut off mid-sentence.

Order matters more than length

Words near the front carry more weight than words near the back. So the fix for a prompt that is not working is usually not to add a clarifier at the end — it is to move the thing you care about to the front.

If the style is what matters, lead with the style. If the subject is what matters, lead with the subject. What you write first is what you get.

Short prompts often beat long ones, especially for people

This surprises people. Faces are where models are most fragile, and a long prompt makes them worse — it crowds out the model's own knowledge of what a face looks like with your adjectives. Ask for a portrait in eight words and you will usually get a better face than in forty.

Use the length you have for things the model cannot guess: the setting, the light, the framing. Do not spend it describing what a person's eyes normally look like.

Do not fight the style you chose

If you pick an illustration style and then write "photorealistic, sharp focus, DSLR", you do not get a compromise — you get a hybrid that looks like neither. The model resolves conflicting instructions by averaging them, and averages of two styles look wrong in a way neither style does.

Pick the style, then describe the content in neutral language and let the style do its job.

A structure that works

Subject first, then setting, then light, then framing. Stop there.

a red fox sitting on a snowy park bench, under a streetlight, at night subject ──────── setting ──────────── light ────────── time

That is fourteen words and it specifies everything that matters. Adding "highly detailed, 8k, masterpiece, award winning" to the end changes almost nothing except pushing something useful past the limit.

Change one thing at a time

When an image is nearly right, resist rewriting the whole prompt. Change a single word and generate again.

This matters more than it sounds, because a word does not adjust the picture — it rewrites the scene. Here is the same prompt four times, with the same seed, changing only the last two words:

a red fox sitting on a park bench under a streetlight, at night a red fox sitting on a park bench under a streetlight, at dawn a red fox sitting on a park bench under a streetlight, in fog a red fox sitting on a park bench under a streetlight, in heavy snow

"At night" gives a tight portrait with the fox facing the camera. "At dawn" pulls the camera right back to a receding street with autumn colour in the trees. "In fog" goes wider still and drops the fox small into the frame. "In heavy snow" adds a second fox that nobody asked for.

Nothing else changed. Not the subject, not the bench, not the random seed. Two words moved the framing, the distance, the palette and the number of animals in the picture.

That is why you change one thing and look. Rewrite five words at once and you cannot tell which one did what — and the next prompt you write will be a guess. Change one, and after a dozen images you are writing prompts that work first time, which no article can teach you directly.

Negative prompts are for exclusion, not quality

A negative prompt steers the model away from things. It is useful for "no text", "not blurry". It is not a quality dial — stacking twenty negative terms does not produce a better picture, and past the same token ceiling the later ones are discarded exactly like positive ones.

title: How to make a custom AI wallpaper for your iPhone
body:
Wallpapers are the easiest win in AI image generation, because the requirements are unusually forgiving: no faces, no text, no anatomy to get wrong. Almost anything the model is good at makes a decent wallpaper.

Think about where the clock sits

This is the thing that separates a wallpaper that works from a picture that happens to be on your phone. The top third of your screen holds the clock and notifications; the bottom third holds the dock and unlock hint. Your image needs to be quiet in both.

So prompt for compositions with a calm top and bottom: a horizon low in the frame, a subject centred with open sky above, a gradient, a texture. Avoid busy detail edge to edge — it will fight everything the system draws on top.

Prompts that reliably work

  • Landscapes with space. Misty mountains at dawn, a lone tree on a hill, a still lake under cloud.
  • Abstract and texture. Flowing liquid colour, marbled stone, brushed metal, layered paper.
  • Night skies. Aurora, a starfield, a city seen from far away.
  • Single objects on plain grounds. One flower, one leaf, one geometric shape.

What to avoid: crowds, text, anything with hands, and dense patterns that make icons hard to read.

Aspect ratio, honestly

Most on-device generators draw square images, because that is what the model was trained on. A phone screen is roughly twice as tall as it is wide. You have two options and one of them is better.

The better one: generate square, then crop to the part you want. You lose some of the image but keep all of its quality. The worse one: stretch it, which distorts everything and always looks it.

Prompt with the crop in mind — put your subject where it will survive being cut down to a tall rectangle.

Make it bigger before you set it

A 768-pixel square looks fine on screen until you crop into it, at which point you are asking a small image to fill a large display. Upscaling before you crop gives the phone more pixels to work with, and the difference is visible on an OLED screen.

Setting it

Save to Photos, open the image, share, then Use as Wallpaper. iOS will let you pan and scale — this is where a taller crop pays off. Check it against both the lock screen and the home screen before you commit; images that look striking on the lock screen sometimes make app icons unreadable at home.

Depth effect

iOS can lift a foreground subject in front of the clock on the lock screen. It works best with a clear single subject against a distinctly separate background — which is another reason to prompt for one object rather than a busy scene.

title: How Stable Diffusion runs on an iPhone or iPad
body:
The short version: the model is converted into Apple's own format, quantized down to a size a phone can hold, and executed on the Neural Engine rather than the GPU. Each of those three steps is doing real work, and skipping any of them puts you back on a server.

Conversion

Models are published as PyTorch weights, which iOS cannot run efficiently. They are converted to Core ML, Apple's format, which lets the system decide which chip should run each operation. This is a translation step, and it is where most attempts fail — an architecture that converts cleanly is a much shorter list than an architecture that exists.

Quantization

An SDXL-class model at full precision is far too large for a phone. Reducing the weights to six bits each cuts the size to roughly a third with a quality cost that is real but small — and, importantly, unevenly distributed. Composition, subject and pose survive essentially untouched; what degrades is fine texture. You give up a little hair detail to make the thing run at all.

Splitting the model up

Even quantized, the largest part of the model exceeds what Core ML will plan in one piece — it fails to build an execution plan and returns an error that does not explain itself. The fix is to split that part into two chunks that are loaded and run in sequence. This detail costs people days when they first meet it.

Running on the Neural Engine

Apple silicon has three places to run this work: the CPU, the GPU, and the Neural Engine. The Neural Engine is slower per operation than the GPU on paper, and better in practice, because it barely heats up. A GPU-based generator throttles noticeably within about a minute of sustained work; the Neural Engine holds its pace. On a device you hold in your hand, that difference decides whether generating five images in a row is pleasant.

Getting there requires the model be converted with an attention implementation the Neural Engine can execute, which is a conversion-time decision rather than something you can switch on later.

Making it fast enough to be worth using

A standard model takes 20 to 50 steps per image. On a phone that is far too slow. Distilled variants — Lightning and Turbo among them — are retrained to produce a comparable image in 4 to 8 steps, which is the difference between seconds and minutes.

They need different settings, and this catches everybody: a distilled model wants a much lower guidance value than the default, around 1.5 rather than 7.5, and a scheduler suited to few steps. Run one at stock settings and you get noise, then conclude the model is broken when it is merely misconfigured.

What you are left with

A model of roughly 3 GB that lives on the device, compiles for the Neural Engine once on first launch — about two minutes, with no way to skip it — and afterwards draws an image in seconds with no network involved at all. You can verify the last part yourself in airplane mode, which is the only claim in this field worth taking on evidence rather than trust.

title: AI image generators with no subscription: what to check before you pay
body:
Almost every AI image app charges monthly, and there is an honest reason for it: most of them are paying a server every time you press the button. If somebody else's computer draws your picture, somebody has to keep paying for that computer.

Which tells you exactly what to look for. An app can only sell you a one-time price if it is not paying per image. That means the model runs on your own phone.

Four things to check before paying anything

  • Does it work in airplane mode? The only test that cannot be faked. Turn off the connection and generate. If it fails, there is a server, and a server means recurring costs that will eventually reach you.
  • Is "unlimited" about quantity or about time? Some apps sell "unlimited" access for a month. Read whether you are buying images or buying days.
  • Does a one-time purchase cover future models? Ask before, not after. An app that charges again for each new model is a subscription with extra steps.
  • Is there a free tier that actually generates? Not a trial that expires — a real number of real images, so you can judge quality before paying.

What one-time pricing costs you

Being fair about the trade: on-device apps ask for a large download, a few gigabytes of storage, and a reasonably recent phone. Subscription apps run on anything with a connection, and their models are usually a generation ahead because they run on hardware nobody could fit in a pocket.

If you generate two images a year, a free cloud tool is the right answer and you should use one. One-time pricing pays off for people who use the thing.

Watch the free built-in options too

Apple's Image Playground is free and built into iOS, and since iOS 27 it produces photorealistic images as well as illustrated ones. Worth knowing that its photorealistic model runs on Apple's servers rather than your phone, so it has usage limits, and more capacity comes with an iCloud+ plan. Free, but metered — and that is the same economics as everything else, just quieter about it.

title: How to create anime and illustrated art from text on your phone
body:
Anime is the most demanding thing to ask a general-purpose image model for, and understanding why will save you a lot of disappointment.

General models versus specialists

A general model has been trained on everything: photographs, paintings, diagrams, illustration. It knows what anime looks like the way a good all-round artist does — well enough to produce something convincing, not well enough to match somebody who draws only that.

A specialist anime model has seen almost nothing else. Its line weight, its eyes, its colour choices are all closer to the real thing. If anime is the only reason you want this, a specialist is worth seeking out.

A general model with a good anime style will make images you are happy with most of the time. It will not fool somebody who spends their evenings in that world.

Prompt shorter than you think

The instinct is to describe the character in exhaustive detail — hair colour, eye colour, outfit, pose, expression, background. Resist it. Long prompts crowd out the model's own sense of the style, and the result drifts towards generic digital art.

Name the subject, name the setting, name the mood. Let the style handle the rest.

a girl with silver hair walking through a rainy neon street subject ───────────── setting ──────────────

Do not ask for photorealism inside an illustrated style

Adding "photorealistic", "8k", "sharp focus" to an anime prompt does not sharpen it. The model averages the two instructions and produces something that is neither — plastic-looking faces on flat backgrounds. Pick one world and stay in it.

Where it will let you down

Hands with the right number of fingers. Two characters interacting. Text on a sign. Consistent features across several images — a model has no memory between generations, so the same prompt gives you a different person each time.

These are limitations of the technology at this size, not of any particular app, and anyone claiming otherwise is selling something.

What works well

Single characters. Scenery and backgrounds, which anime models render beautifully. Mood pieces — rain, neon, sunset, snow. Wallpapers, which is what most people end up making.

title: On-device or cloud AI image generation: which should you use?
body:
These are not competing versions of the same thing. They are different trades, and which one is right depends on facts about you rather than facts about the technology.

Use cloud if…

  • You want the best possible image. Server models are larger than anything that fits on a phone, and it shows in prompt-following and in fine detail.
  • You need text inside the picture. Cloud models render lettering far more reliably. On-device models are poor at it.
  • Your device is older. Cloud runs on anything with a connection.
  • You generate rarely. A free tier covers occasional use and costs nothing.

Use on-device if…

  • You want to generate a lot. No counter, no queue. Running out is not a thing that happens.
  • You are somewhere without a connection. A plane, a train, a basement, abroad without roaming.
  • The subject matter is private. Photos of your family, work in progress, anything you would rather not upload. It cannot leak from a server it never reached.
  • You dislike subscriptions. On-device generation costs the developer nothing per image, which is the only reason a one-time price is possible at all.

The honest summary of the quality gap

A phone-sized model is roughly a generation behind a server model. That gap is real, and it shows most in complicated prompts, in text, and in hands. It shows least in single subjects, landscapes, textures and mood — which is most of what people actually make.

Where the free built-in option sits

Apple's Image Playground is worth knowing about because it is already on your phone. Since iOS 27 it does photorealistic images as well as illustrated ones, and for occasional use it is free and very good. Two things to know: the photorealistic model runs on Apple's servers, so it needs a connection and comes with usage limits, and the whole feature requires an A17 Pro chip or newer. On older hardware it is not available at all.

That last point catches people out. Some phones that are too old for Apple's own tool can still run a third-party on-device generator, because the memory requirements and the chip requirements are not the same thing.

title: Image Playground and third-party generators: what each is for
body:
Apple's Image Playground is free, built into iOS, and since iOS 27 it makes photorealistic pictures as well as illustrated ones. For a lot of people that is the end of the question, and it should be — start there before paying anyone for anything.

What Image Playground is very good at

It is already installed. It is free. It is woven into Messages and Notes, so making a picture and sending it is one gesture. Genmoji is genuinely delightful and nothing else does it. The illustrated styles are polished and consistent, and the whole thing is designed so you cannot really get a bad result.

What it does not do

  • It needs a recent device. An A17 Pro chip or newer on iPhone, or M-series on iPad. An iPhone 14 cannot run it at all.
  • Its photorealistic model runs on Apple's servers. That means a connection is required and there are usage limits, with more capacity attached to iCloud+ plans.
  • It is deliberately narrow. Apple has drawn firm lines about what it will draw, which is a reasonable choice for something shipped to everybody, and a limitation if you are outside those lines.
  • It does not edit your existing photos in the way a general image model can — restyling a picture you took, or enlarging one.

When a third-party on-device app makes sense

When you want to generate a lot without a counter. When you are frequently offline. When your phone is a couple of years old and Apple's tool is not offered to you. When you want many styles rather than a few. When you want to work on photographs you already have.

When it does not

If you have a current iPhone, a normal connection, and you make a handful of pictures a month, Image Playground is free and will do it. Paying for a third-party app in that situation buys you very little.

They also coexist quite happily

Genmoji in Messages, something else when you want a lot of images or no connection. Nobody has to pick a side — the trades are different enough that plenty of people reasonably use both.
